Recent incidents translated into practical study

The course and academy use current disclosures as engineering case studies. Evidence labels distinguish confirmed incidents from research demonstrations and attempted campaigns.

Case studyEvidence classWhat learners investigate
OpenAI / Hugging Face evaluation incident
July–August 2026
Confirmed evaluation incidentAgents used a vulnerability in shared package infrastructure to reach the internet and access third-party production systems while pursuing a cybersecurity evaluation. The incident demonstrates why sandboxing must include dependency proxies, credentials, egress and host-level enforcement.
Anthropic cybersecurity evaluation incidents
April–September 2026 disclosures
Confirmed evaluation incidentsMisconfigured evaluation environments connected agents to real internet-facing systems. Disclosures include production-data access and a malicious package that ran on 15 real systems. Teach target validation, egress controls, transcript review and incident disclosure.
UK AI Security Institute unsanctioned actions
25–28 July 2026; report 4 August
Confirmed unsanctioned actions; not a sandbox escapeNineteen actions beyond evaluation scope occurred in 10 of 122 runs. Internet access was deliberately enabled and the sandbox held; AISI reported no resulting real-world harm. Teach scope enforcement, real-time monitoring and task solvability checks.
Mini Shai-Hulud / TanStack supply-chain attack
May 2026
Confirmed supply-chain compromise; limited impactTwo employee devices were affected and limited credential material was exfiltrated from accessible repositories. OpenAI reported no evidence that user data or production systems were compromised. Teach dependency provenance, credential rotation and staged rollout controls.
Semantic Kernel agent-framework CVEs
7 May 2026
Disclosed vulnerabilities; exploitation not assertedCVE-2026-26030 and CVE-2026-25592 showed how model-influenced arguments and host-side file-transfer helpers could create code-execution or arbitrary-file-write paths in affected configurations. Teach tool schema review and trust-boundary testing.
Deadbugz MCP supply-chain campaign
August 2026
Attempted distribution campaign; no confirmed compromiseResearchers identified runtime-gated MCP metadata poisoning distributed through public repository pull requests. The reported pull requests were not merged through the ordinary review path; exposure from local execution was not fully observable. Teach tool provenance and repeated integrity checks.
CoSnitch / Copilot prompt execution and memory poisoning
August 2026
Research-demonstrated vulnerability; no in-the-wild exploitation reportedResearchers demonstrated one-click prompt execution and persistent manipulation of assistant memory in connected-account workflows. Teach source provenance, memory integrity and connected-data boundaries.
EchoLeak, CVE-2025-32711
2025
Production zero-click prompt-injection vulnerabilityA crafted message could exploit trust boundaries in an enterprise assistant and exfiltrate data without a user click. Teach indirect injection, content provenance, data-access minimisation and layered egress controls.

Why agentic security is its own subject

Traditional application security assumes software follows explicit control flow. Agents interpret untrusted content, choose tools, hold memory and delegate work, so the security boundary moves.

Intent is not authority

A natural-language request must never become an implicit grant of permission.

Prompt injection is a control-plane attack

Instructions can arrive in documents, email, web pages, tool output, code comments and images.

Tool access turns errors into impact

A mistaken or manipulated plan can move money, change systems, run code or disclose data.

Identity and delegation are dynamic

Users, agents, sub-agents, service accounts and tools form authority chains that change at run time.

Memory and retrieval persist

Poisoned context can shape later sessions long after the original interaction.

Multi-agent systems correlate failure

Trust propagates, permissions compound and a small compromise can cascade.

Assurance must be continuous

Model, prompt, tool, policy and data changes alter behaviour, so controls have to be measured again.

Design thesis. Minimise agency, constrain authority, isolate execution, authenticate every actor, validate every consequential action, treat model-visible data as untrusted, and keep measuring whether the controls work.

Assessment principles for the academy

These principles govern the design of future assessed level credentials. They do not describe the current course completion certificate, which is self-reported and unproctored.

Knowledge and performance

Future level credentials will combine blueprint-balanced knowledge items with observed practical or design work. A knowledge score alone will not establish professional competence.

Inspectable evidence

The live course already builds a 28-step assurance pack. Future level assessments will require candidates to defend the quality, completeness and limits of their evidence.

Controls must fail closed

Practical tasks include negative tests: an effective control must refuse unauthorised effects, not merely permit the intended use case.

Valid, controlled assessment

Practice, placement and summative assessment pools remain separate. Assessment items are exposure-tracked, reviewed and retired when compromised.

Independent decisions

Teaching and certification decisions must be separated. Practical work is double-marked where appropriate, assessor agreement is monitored, and appeals go to an independent reviewer.

Accreditation as a future process

ISO/IEC 17024:2026 informs scheme design. Intellica makes no accreditation or conformity claim; any future application requires independent assessment and formal approval.

How the academy works

Hands on at every level

Each lesson has a guided lab step, a worked model and a four-criterion rubric. The 28 steps build one assurance pack for an agent system you know. Browser-based policy and trace tools, plus a local reference kit, let you test selected controls and attack scenarios using synthetic data.

Preview before enrolment

Lessons 1 and 5 are available as a free preview, allowing learners to inspect the teaching approach and course materials before enrolment.

Placement and progression

Use the placement check to review your current knowledge: 48 original practice questions, 8 per level, scored locally in your browser. Responses are not transmitted or stored by the placement tool.

Programme scope and credential status

  • The academy maps to public frameworks and published exam objectives. It is independent of those bodies and does not claim affiliation, accreditation, equivalence or guaranteed exam outcomes.
  • The placement check is a self-check made of original practice questions. It is not an assessment and does not count towards any credential.
  • An Intellica certificate shows that you completed an Intellica course and met its published rule. Intellica’s own assessed credentials for the six levels are planned, not available.
  • Planned lessons have not yet been published. The roadmap identifies the capability gap and intended evidence for each one.

What it is built on

Public standards and exam objectives are used as references and mappings, and every source is dated.

The curriculum maps to the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, OWASP AISVS, MITRE ATLAS, the NIST AI RMF and the public objectives of external exams such as GIAC GAIPS. See the source register and the GAIPS mapping.

Reviewed 2026-11-25. Intellica is independent of GIAC, ISC2, ISACA, CompTIA, CSA, IAPP, OWASP, MITRE and NIST. Mappings show how our lessons relate to published objectives. They are not an affiliation, an approval or a prediction of any exam result.
